name: read-write-lock
intent: Permit any number of concurrent readers or exactly one writer over the same shared mutable state, so read-dominated workloads stop excluding each other while writers still observe and produce a consistent view.
problem: Shared mutable state that is read by many threads and modified rarely is guarded by a single mutual-exclusion lock, so every reader serialises behind every other reader even though reads do not conflict with each other. The recurring decision is how to remove that self-inflicted queue: keep the exclusive lock and accept that read-mostly access scales no better than write-mostly access, split the state so each part gets its own lock, or use a lock that understands the two conflict relations - readers share, writers exclude - so concurrent readers proceed while a writer waits for them all and blocks new ones.
context: In-process shared mutable state accessed from multiple OS threads or blocking tasks: caches, registries, routing and lookup tables, symbol tables, in-memory indexes and configuration snapshots where reads dominate by a wide margin and write sections are rare. It applies when acquisition can block the caller for the duration of a read or write section, when the runtime ships a reader-writer primitive or the pieces to build one (a mutex plus a condition variable), and when the access modes can be expressed as distinct read and write operations. It fits badly with single-threaded runtimes, with async runtimes that must not block a task thread, with state shared across processes, and with designs that remove the shared mutable read path entirely (immutable snapshots, copy-on-write, RCU).
benefits: Read-side parallelism: readers no longer exclude each other, so a read-mostly workload's throughput can scale with cores where a plain mutex queues every reader behind the previous one.
Writers still see consistency: a writer waits for the readers to finish and blocks new readers while it holds the lock, so the mutation is observed atomically.
The two conflict relations become part of the API: shared read and exclusive write are separate operations, so access policy is visible at the call site instead of hidden behind one blanket lock.
Contention is reduced exactly where it is most expensive: the dominant operation (reading) is the cheap one, so the queue that forms is over writes, which read-mostly designs already keep rare.
The priority policy is explicit and pluggable: fair versus non-fair, read-preferring versus write-preferring versus phase-fair is a construction-time choice, not an accident of the scheduler.
It composes with the rest of the synchronisation toolkit: the same lock works under Scoped Locking/RAII release discipline, and a read lock may be held across the protected object's read-only calls.

Where the platform supports it, it offers a safe upgrade path: a dedicated upgradeable mode (C#) or a convert/validate operation (StampedLock) lets a caller check then write without dropping the guarantee.

Phase-fair variants ( Brandenburg & Anderson, ECRTS 2009 ) offer O(1) worst-case read blocking regardless of the number of waiting writers, avoiding the scalability collapse that plagues reader- and writer-preference locks under high contention.
tradeoffs: It is noticeably more complex than a mutex: reader counting, an active-writer flag, waiting-reader and waiting-writer accounting and a re-check loop, all of which must be correct or the lock silently mis-synchronises.
Every access pays extra bookkeeping, so with short sections or a high write ratio a reader-writer lock is slower than a plain mutex — concurrency machinery that reduces throughput.

The priority policy is a real design decision with failure modes: read-preferring implementations can starve writers indefinitely, while fair or write-preferring ones queue readers behind waiting writers and give back much of the read parallelism that justified the lock.

Upgrades are not portable: Java and Go forbid read-to-write upgrade, StampedLock is non-reentrant, POSIX offers no upgrade at all; callers must release the read lock, re-acquire the write lock and re-validate, which is easy to get wrong.
It tempts callers into longer critical sections: because reads 'do not conflict', read locks are held across work that should not be under any lock.

Exposing distinct read and write access publishes the lock: collaborators must know which mode to take, which couples them to the synchronisation strategy and makes the protected object harder to replace.

It is a shared-memory answer: it does not survive process boundaries, it blocks threads (hostile to event loops and some async runtimes), and immutable snapshots, copy-on-write or RCU often scale reads better with no reader-side lock at all.
Deadlocks remain available: recursion rules differ per language and implementation, and lock-ordering across two reader-writer locks is no safer than with plain mutexes.

The hot reader-count word becomes a cache-line contention point on multi-socket NUMA machines; per-CPU sharded RWLocks (e.g., Linux percpu_rwsem) or RCU eliminate this at the cost of more complex writes.
Under high read-only contention, phase-fair locks can degrade to mutex-like performance when readers and writers are heavily interleaved in the wait queue.

participants.responsibility: The synchronisation object; owns the reader count, the active-writer flag and the waiting readers and writers, and enforces the invariant 'any number of readers or one writer, never both' on every acquisition.
Acquires shared access and proceeds concurrently with other readers; must not mutate the protected state and must release the read lock on every exit path.
Acquires exclusive access once all readers and other writers have left, mutates the protected state and blocks new readers for the duration; never attempts to upgrade a read lock it is still holding.

Decides which side wins when readers and writers contend (read-preferring, write-preferring/fair, phase-fair, arrival ordered) and therefore which side can starve; usually fixed at construction time via a fair flag, an OS attribute or the choice of lock library. Phase-fair (Brandenburg & Anderson 2009) alternates reader and writer phases and provides O(1) read blocking regardless of writer queue length.

The contract that lets a caller change modes safely: a dedicated upgradeable mode where the platform offers one (C# UpgradeableReadLock), otherwise release-and-re-acquire plus re-validation, and downgrade only where the platform guarantees it (Java write→read downgrade is safe).

use_cases: Read-mostly in-memory caches and lookup tables (route tables, feature-flag snapshots, configuration) where the request path reads constantly and a background task refreshes rarely.
In-memory indexes and symbol tables: query operations run concurrently while insert, remove or rebuild happens occasionally.
Registries and service directories consulted on every request and updated by registration and deregistration events.
Data structures with long read-only phases and occasional bulk updates: analytics state snapshots, in-memory graphs reloaded periodically.
Read sections that legitimately block or compute (reading a shared file handle, decoding a shared buffer) where serialising those readers would dominate the schedule.
In-process shared state that one dedicated writer thread mutates while many worker threads read it, as in half-sync/half-async or master-worker designs.
DNS caches and service-discovery registries (e.g., etcd client caches, Consul KV store replicas) where reads dominate and updates propagate via gossip or periodic sync.
Configuration management systems: feature flags, feature toggles, tenant routing rules read on every request and reloaded on config-change events.
Database connection pools and session caches: connection state is read constantly but created/destroyed rarely.
Pub/sub topic subscription tables: subscriber routing is read-heavy, topic creation/deletion is occasional.

Rate limiters and counters: token buckets and sliding-window counters read per-request and updated per-arrival, but the read path can be made lock-free with atomics — a RWLock fits the write-heavy update variant.
In-memory search indexes (Lucene segments, SQLite FTS tables): queries are concurrent-read, updates are batched and infrequent.

Real-time notification services: every incoming event must match a shared subscription lookup table; events are frequent, table changes are rare — RWLock avoids serialising every match operation ( Gore et al. 2004 ).
Network routing tables in routers/load balancers: looked up for every packet/request, updated only on topology changes.
Compiled regex or protocol descriptor caches: expensive to build, read on every request, rebuilt rarely.
Java StampedLock optimistic-read fallback: for read-heavy workloads where contention is low, optimistic reads validate cheaply and avoid all lock acquisition overhead on the common uncontended path.

Go's sync.RWMutex is a concrete fit for a read-mostly in-process map or cache: concurrent RLock calls share, while Lock excludes readers; its documented no-upgrade and no-copy-after-first-use contracts must shape the API.

Java's java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock fits shared indexes and caches when callers need explicit read/write modes, while StampedLock adds an optimistic-read path; Oracle documents safe write-to-read downgrades but no read-to-write upgrade.

.NET System.Threading.ReaderWriterLockSlim fits conditional cache or configuration insertion: many readers share, exactly one UpgradeableRead holder may enter Write, and each mode must be exited reliably.
avoid_when: The state fits an immutable value or can be published as an immutable snapshot: readers then need no lock at all (copy-on-write, RCU, atomic pointer swap), which scales reads better.
Writes are not rare: a write-heavy workload turns the reader-writer lock into a mutex with extra overhead and policy pitfalls — use a plain mutex, or confine the state per thread or per shard.
Sections are tiny (a few field reads): the bookkeeping costs more than the contention it avoids, and a plain mutex or atomics are faster and simpler.

The runtime is single-threaded or non-blocking by design (browser/Node event loop, an async executor that must not block its threads): use single-owner state plus message passing or an async-aware mutex instead.
The invariant spans processes or nodes: use a database transaction, an optimistic concurrency/version check or a distributed lock — an in-process reader-writer lock gives no cross-process guarantee.
A dominant runtime primitive already fits: lock striping (shard the state), guarded suspension (a handoff), or the atomic operations of a concurrent collection.
The platform already provides the guarantee (MVCC stores, database engines, the OS's own read-copy-update mechanism).
Read operations are sub-microsecond and the workload is write-balanced: RWLock overhead (30–50 ns per acquire) exceeds the actual work; a plain mutex wins.

The data is too large to clone cheaply but reads must scale to dozens of cores on NUMA: the shared reader-count cache line becomes a contention bottleneck — use per-CPU sharded RWLocks or RCU instead.
Writes require predictable low-latency completion: RCU grace periods (1–10 ms) are unacceptable and the data cannot be copied cheaply — RWLock with bounded critical sections is preferable.
anti_patterns: Hand-rolling a reader-writer lock over a mutex and a condition variable without a re-check loop, so a notification that does not make the predicate true either proceeds unsafely or is lost.
Attempting to upgrade an already-held read lock into a write lock in place: it deadlocks whenever two readers both try (and is undefined or EDEADLK on POSIX), yet it is the single most common misuse.
Holding a read lock across slow work or user callbacks 'because readers do not block each other', turning the write path into a stop-the-world pause.
Using a reader-writer lock where every operation needs the write lock (a write-heavy reload), paying the policy and bookkeeping cost for nothing.
Read-preferring policy plus a steady reader stream: writers starve indefinitely, the cache never refreshes, and the failure looks like a hang rather than a lock bug.
Re-publishing the lock: the protected object exposes read/write acquisition to callers, so the synchronisation strategy leaks into every caller and cannot be changed.
Recursive read-locking in implementations that forbid it (Go's RWMutex blocks a second RLock while a writer waits) presented as safe reentrancy.
Go RWMutex reentrancy: nesting RLock calls within a read section, then calling a function that also acquires RLock — if a writer is waiting the inner RLock deadlocks.
Reader starvation in write-preferring mode: a steady stream of write lock acquisitions (each short) can indefinitely queue-jump ahead of waiting readers, making reads appear to hang.

Python RWLock without writer priority: a third-party recipe that defaults to reader-preferring starves writers silently under I/O-bound read traffic — always use writer-preferring or fair as the production default.

Lock-ordering deadlock across two RW locks: thread A holds lock X in read mode and lock Y in write mode while thread B holds lock Y in read mode and tries to acquire lock X in write mode — same circular-dependency problem as plain mutexes.
Using a RWLock in Python where every 'read' releases the GIL anyway (I/O, ctypes call) — the lock adds overhead but no parallelism benefit for that specific operation.

RWLock use in a NUMA multi-socket machine under high read contention: the shared reader-count cache line bounces across sockets, costing 100+ ns per acquire and making 32-thread reads slower than 4-thread reads.

Relying on platform defaults for priority policy without documenting it: Linux glibc pthread_rwlock is reader-preferring, BSD/macOS is writer-preferring — the same code can starve writers on Linux or readers on macOS.
Using a read-heavy RWLock on a runtime that does not parallelize CPU work (Python GIL, browser JS main thread): the lock adds overhead but the work is still serialized.
design_principles: Separate the two conflict relations (read-read compatible, write-everything exclusive) instead of serialising all access on one relation.
Make the concurrency policy an explicit construction-time decision rather than an implementation accident.
Least privilege of access mode: give each caller the weakest mode that lets it do its work — read where possible, write only where needed.
Keep the critical section scoped to the invariant it protects: acquire on entry, release on every exit path (Scoped Locking).
Prefer removing shared mutable state over synchronising it: immutability, ownership transfer and message passing eliminate the lock class entirely.
Design the lock around the contention profile: shard the data (lock striping) before reaching for fancier locking.
Prefer platform-provided RWLock primitives over hand-rolled condition-variable implementations; correctness of hand-rolled locks is notoriously hard to verify.
Treat the priority policy as a production concern: writer-preferring or phase-fair is almost always the right default; reader-preferring only in controlled benchmarks.
Measure before adopting: the break-even point is approximately when read work is at least 10× the RWLock overhead (~300 ns on x86); below that a plain mutex is faster.
For cross-language teams: document the priority policy explicitly (e.g., 'writer-preferring') rather than relying on platform defaults that differ.
Prefer lock-free alternatives (Arc + atomic swap, RCU) when reads vastly outnumber writes and data is copyable — the reader path can be reduced to a single atomic load.
Treat the lock's cache-line behavior as a first-class performance concern on NUMA systems; profile the reader-count hot spot under multi-socket contention.
best_practices: Acquire and release read locks with RAII or scoped constructs (shared_lock, using, try/finally, with_read_lock) so no error path can leak a read lock and block the next writer forever.

Never upgrade a read lock in place; release it, take the write lock and re-validate the state, or use a dedicated upgradeable mode where the language offers one (C# UpgradeableRead, boost::upgrade_mutex, Java downgrade pattern).
Choose the priority policy deliberately: writer-preferring or phase-fair to avoid writer starvation (the usual production choice), arrival order for maximum throughput when starvation is acceptable.
Keep read critical sections short and free of blocking I/O, unknown callbacks and lock acquisition; the read path must be safe by construction, not by accident.
Segment the protected state (shards, stripes, partitions) so readers scale without contending on a single lock word.
Prefer immutable snapshots and copy-on-write for massively read-dominated state, reserving the reader-writer lock for state that must mutate in place.
Instrument and measure: track read/write hold times and waiter counts, and revisit the choice when the write ratio rises.
Document who may take which mode, and that intra-component calls must not re-acquire the lock, so recursive acquisition hazards are visible (Thread-Safe Interface).

In Go: always use defer Unlock immediately after acquiring Lock/RLock — never manually unlock at scattered exit points. Pass sync.RWMutex by pointer when storing it in a struct. Prefer sync.Mutex unless reads are ≥90% of operations.

In Java: wrap every lock/unlock pair in try/finally. Prefer the ReentrantReadWriteLock constructor's fair parameter if the application cannot tolerate indefinite starvation. Use the downgrade pattern (write → read → release write) for cache coherence after updates. Consider StampedLock.tryOptimisticRead() for the uncontended read-heavy path.

In C#: prefer LockRecursionPolicy.NoRecursion (the default and recommended setting). Use UpgradeableReadLock to handle the read-then-maybe-write pattern safely without a deadlock window. Only one thread can hold UpgradeableRead at a time — structure code so upgradeable sections are brief and non-overlapping.

In Python: do not assume a third-party RWLock recipe has the same semantics as Java's or Go's — read the source. Prefer well-maintained packages (e.g., readerwriterlock on PyPI) over hand-rolled Condition-based code. Be aware that due to the GIL, an RWLock on CPU-bound read sections provides no throughput gain over a plain threading.Lock — it only helps for I/O-bound reads or sections that call out to C extensions.

For cross-language teams: document the priority policy explicitly (e.g., 'writer-preferring') rather than relying on platform defaults that differ (Go defaults writer-preferring, Java non-fair defaults to no specific preference, C# fair mode is opt-in, Linux glibc pthread_rwlock is reader-preferring).
Add timeouts to lock acquisitions in server loops or request-handling paths: a stuck writer can turn into a distributed denial of service against the local process. Track timeout events as a metric.
When migrating from a plain mutex: benchmark first. If the critical section is short or the workload is write-heavy, the extra bookkeeping of an RWLock makes it slower than a mutex.

On NUMA systems: prefer per-CPU sharded RWLocks (Linux percpu_rwsem semantics) or RCU over a single shared reader-count word, which becomes a cache-line ping-pong bottleneck under high read contention.
For real-time systems: prefer phase-fair RWLock (Brandenburg & Anderson 2009) over reader- or writer-preference variants; it provides O(1) read blocking regardless of waiting writer queue length.
Where upgrade is needed but not natively supported (Python, generic C): use a separate upgradeable-lock concept (a mutex held only during the upgrade window) rather than attempting in-place upgrade.
Rust: prefer parking_lot::RwLock over std::sync::RwLock. For read-mostly data that is cheap to clone, prefer Arc + ArcSwap (no reader-side lock) over RwLock entirely.
Swift: prefer Swift actors (isolated state) over manual RWLock for new code. Use dispatch barrier queues for concurrent read / exclusive write semantics on Darwin platforms.
sources: Lea, D., Concurrent Programming in Java: Design Principles and Patterns, 2nd ed. (Addison-Wesley, 1999) — section 2.5.2 'Read-Write Locks' (the catalog's originating citation).
Mellor-Crummey, J. and Scott, M., 'Algorithms for Scalable Synchronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors', ACM TOCS, 1991 — reader-writer spin locks for multiprocessors, phase-fair lock design.

Brandenburg, B. and Anderson, J., 'Spin-based Reader-Writer Synchronization for Multiprocessor Real-Time Systems', Real-Time Systems, 46(1):25–87, 2010 — phase-fair RW locks, O(1) read blocking, schedulability analysis.

Brandenburg, B. and Anderson, J., 'Reader-Writer Synchronization for Shared-Memory Multiprocessor Real-Time Systems', ECRTS 2009 — first phase-fair lock formalization and evaluation against preference/task-fair locks.
Davidson, B. et al., 'Scalable Reader-Writer Locks', SPAA 2009 — OLL locks (GOLL, FOLL, ROLL) using C-SNZI for near-perfect read scalability under high read-only contention.
Brandenburg, B., 'The OMLP Family of Optimal Multiprocessor Real-Time Locking Protocols', 2012 — PF-L phase-fair lock with O(1) amortized RMR complexity per read request.

Ward, B. and Anderson, J., 'Multi-Resource Real-Time Reader/Writer Locks for Multiprocessors', RTSS 2013 — R/W RNLP, first fine-grained multiprocessor RW locking protocol supporting concurrent read/write on different resources.

Nemitz, C. et al., 'Light Reading: Optimizing Reader/Writer Locking for Read-Dominant Real-Time Workloads', ECRTS 2021 — new RW locking implementation with up to 70% overhead reduction and 450% read throughput improvement over prior art.
Brandwaj, A. and Salah, A., 'Process Synchronization with Readers and Writers Revisited', 2014 — starvation-free semaphore-based RW lock algorithm achieving combined fairness (Fairness-3).
Baker, T. et al., 'Reader-Writer Synchronization for Shared-Memory Multiprocessor Real-Time Systems', ECRTS 2009 — phase-fair RW locks for real-time systems.

Lamport, L., 'Concurrent Reading and Writing', Communications of the ACM, 1977 — foundational paper establishing the impossibility of wait-free concurrent read-write access without special hardware assumptions, and the minimum requirements for safe readers-writers synchronisation.

Jayanti, P. and Liu, S., 'Reader-Writer Exclusion Supporting Upgrade and Downgrade with Starvation Freedom', Dartmouth College, 2016 — starvation-free RW exclusion supporting dynamic upgrade/downgrade.
The Linux Kernel, 'What is RCU?', https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/RCU/whatisRCU.html — RCU (Read-Copy-Update) as an alternative to reader-writer locks for extreme read-mostly workloads.

The Linux Kernel, 'Sequence counters and sequential locks', https://docs.kernel.org/6.17/locking/seqlock.html — seqlock as a lockless-reader alternative to RW locks for small, frequently-updated data.
Upstash, 'Upgradable RWLock for Go', https://upstash.com/blog/upgradable-rwlock-for-go — upgradable-read lock pattern for Go to solve the long-read-phase blocking writers problem.
